summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: criminal law, identity documents, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here in the same terms. No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor.

Legal gender-marker change has been available since 1 January 2017 without surgery, sterilisation, psychiatric certificate or medical diagnosis, on application to a court, while a first-name change can be made at the registry office. Gender-affirming hormone therapy has been available under French law since 1975 and gender-affirming surgery was legalised in 1979. Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited by article 225-1 of the Penal Code, amended on 18 November 2016 to replace the earlier wording of "sexual identity", and by Chapter 2 of the Labour Code, which bars exclusion from recruitment, internships and training, sanction, dismissal and other discriminatory measures on that ground. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide, including overseas territories, since 2013, with joint adoption.

Conversion practices are a criminal offence carrying up to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 30,000 euros, under a bill passed by the Senate on 7 December 2020, concurring with the National Assembly on 25 January 2022 and published on 1 February 2022. Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating circumstance for every crime punishable by imprisonment.

Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival.

Detainees held in Saint Barthélemy fall under the French prison administration, in which the controller-general of detention places has found that trans detainees, overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement, suffer the most severe consequences of custody; administration policy recognises only biological sex, and a 2011 case in Nantes placed a trans woman in a men's prison. The controller-general's opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on about 40 referrals since 2010, finds that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention and issues recommendations that apply equally to intersex and non-binary people.

The island's documented social environment carries little visible risk: about 8 square miles with a small resident population, an economy built on luxury yachting and high-end tourism where discretion is the norm, couples read locally as same-sex attracting no attention, and no hostility toward LGBTQ visitors is recorded. There are no LGBTQ venues and no Pride-specific events, and hospitality staff are trained for diverse guests.

Gender-affirming care reaches an island with limited healthcare access, which an international LGBT+ rights index records as the single red flag against nine positive rights in an overall rating of 7.7 out of 10.
tangentialFactors:
Saint Barthélemy's joint deputy with Saint Martin was among 11 deputies representing outlying constituencies who voted against the 2013 same-sex marriage law, even though that law applies in full here. The vote indicates a local political current that the island's social climate does not otherwise express.

Travel guides describe Saint Barthélemy's reputation as an international celebrity destination as having produced a more open and relaxed social climate for LGBTQ people than other French Caribbean territories, and note that Guadeloupe, Martinique and Saint Martin have gay bars, discos, saunas and beaches while Saint Barthélemy has none. The comparison describes an absence of a visible scene rather than a difference in legal standing, since the same national framework governs all of them.

Discretion is the operative norm rather than visible affirmation: visitors are high-end and discreet, there is no Pride-specific event, and the assessment of safety rests on low crime and an accepting culture rather than on documented protections being tested locally.
localsOnly:
Residents change their legal gender marker by application to a court, while a first-name change is handled at the registry office. Neither step requires surgery, sterilisation, a psychiatrist's certificate or a medical diagnosis.

Residents covered by the national long-term illness scheme keep transsexualism listed under ALD 31, with treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale. Access to that care is documented nationally as subject to extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, which bears directly on a small island population.

Residents have anti-discrimination recourse under article 225-1 of the Penal Code and Chapter 2 of the Labour Code, and transphobia operates as an aggravating circumstance in criminal proceedings. Non-binary residents have no legal recognition, and a resident held in custody is placed under the French prison administration's biological-sex policy.

Community life offers no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention in ordinary settings, and discretion is the local convention across the island's tourism economy.
outOfScopeNotes:
No government LGBT+ travel advice exists for Saint Barthélemy, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office shows no warnings for the territory. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted, so the assessment rests on legal texts, the rights index and travel reporting rather than on visitor accounts.

Whether the court with jurisdiction over a gender-marker application sits on the island or requires travel to France is not sourced here.

Whether the recommendations in the controller-general's 2021 opinion have been implemented in the detention facilities serving Saint Barthélemy is not sourced. The opinion's findings are drawn from referrals across the French system as a whole.

Local enforcement data for the anti-discrimination statute, including complaints filed on the island and their outcomes, is not sourced. Availability of gender-affirming care on the island itself is likewise not sourced beyond the index's "limited healthcare access" flag.

The 7.7 out of 10 rating is a composite of nine positive rights and one red flag; the index's weighting methodology is not reproduced here, and no trans-specific incidents of violence against visitors are recorded in the sources.
